sections.content:
## What You'll Learn

The AI ecosystem has exploded. There are tools for chat, search, images, audio, video, writing, coding, research, and dozens of other categories — and new ones launch every week. By the end of this lesson you'll be able to name the major categories, understand why different tools exist for different jobs, and know which ones to try first.

You won't need to learn every tool. You need to know the landscape well enough to reach for the right one — and to recognise when a new tool you haven't heard of is genuinely novel vs. a slight variation on something you already know.

## The Landscape at a Glance (2026)

AI tools aren't competing for the same job — they're built for fundamentally different tasks. Here's the current map:

| Category | What it does | Leading tools |
|----------|--------------|---------------|
| **Chat / general assistant** | Conversation, writing, analysis, reasoning | Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini |
| **AI search** | Web search with cited sources | Perplexity, Bing Copilot |
| **Deep research** | Systematic multi-source research | Perplexity Deep Research, ChatGPT Deep Research |
| **Academic research** | Scientific literature search | Elicit, Consensus, Scite |
| **Image generation** | Create images from text | DALL-E, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion |
| **Audio & music** | Generate speech, music, transcription | ElevenLabs, Suno, Whisper |
| **Video generation** | Create short video from text/images | Sora, Google Veo 3, Runway, Kling |
| **Knowledge base / RAG** | Chat with your own documents | NotebookLM, Claude Projects |
| **Presentations** | Slides from a prompt or document | Gamma, Canva AI, PowerPoint Copilot |
| **Writing assistant** | Improve drafts, grammar, tone | Grammarly AI, Notion AI, Jasper |
| **Coding assistant** | Write and explain code | Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor |
| **Automation** | Connect apps, build no-code workflows | Zapier, n8n, Make |
| **AI agents** | Autonomous multi-step task completion | Claude Research, Perplexity Deep Research |
| **Local AI** | Run models on your own machine | Ollama, LM Studio |
| **Meeting AI** | Transcribe, summarise meetings | Otter.ai, Fireflies, Teams Copilot |
| **Enterprise AI suite** | AI across email, docs, spreadsheets, meetings | Microsoft 365 Copilot, Google Workspace AI |

This table will mean more to you as you work through the course — you'll use tools from most of these categories. For now, treat it as a reference map.

## The Big Three — Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini

The three dominant general-purpose AI assistants each have different strengths. Understanding these differences helps you choose the right one for each task.

**Claude (Anthropic)**
- Strongest: instruction-following, long-form writing, complex analysis, coding (Sonnet 4.6 leads SWE-bench Verified at 79.6% as of 2026)
- Context window: 200K tokens (Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.8 standard); 1M token context in beta — Claude Fable 5 (the most capable tier) has adaptive thinking always on
- Notable: Claude Code (CLI tool) for developers; Projects feature for persistent context; multiple model tiers (Haiku 4.5 / Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.8 / Fable 5)
- Best for: writing, coding, analysis, anything where you need precise instruction-following

**ChatGPT / GPT-5 (OpenAI)**
- Strongest: multimodal (image + voice input/output), broadest third-party ecosystem, Code Interpreter for data analysis, DALL-E image generation
- Context window: 1M+ tokens (GPT-5); model family spans GPT-5 (flagship), o3/o4-mini (reasoning models), and budget options down to GPT-4.1 nano
- Notable: GPT Store has thousands of custom AI tools; Deep Research mode for comprehensive reports; ChatGPT Plus at $20/month
- Best for: image analysis, voice interaction, data analysis in Code Interpreter, generating images with DALL-E

**Gemini (Google)**
- Strongest: live web search built-in (always current), 1M token context window, Google Workspace integration (Gmail, Docs, Sheets), native video and audio understanding
- Context window: up to 1,000,000 tokens (Gemini 2.5 Pro) — can hold an entire book in context; Gemini 2.5 Flash-Lite for budget/high-volume tasks
- Notable: Native integration into Google apps; Gemini 2.5 Flash includes thinking/reasoning capabilities; flash image generation and editing (Gemini 2.5 Flash Image)
- Best for: processing enormous documents, real-time factual questions, Google Workspace users, video/audio analysis

**The practical takeaway:** If you only use one: start with Claude for quality of reasoning and writing. Add Gemini if you're in Google Workspace. Add ChatGPT for image analysis, data analysis, or voice features.

## Why Different Tools for Different Jobs

You might wonder: if Claude can write text, why does Perplexity exist? If ChatGPT can answer questions, why use Elicit? The answer is that these tools are optimised for different constraints.

**General chat AI** (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini) is optimised for flexible, open-ended conversation. It can do almost anything with text — but it doesn't cite sources by default, and its knowledge has a training cutoff.

**AI search** (Perplexity) is optimised for factual research with citations. Every answer links back to the source — you can click through and verify. For anything where currency and verifiability matter, Perplexity is the right tool, not Claude.

**Academic research tools** (Elicit, Consensus, Scite) search specifically over peer-reviewed literature. They don't search the general web — they search databases of scientific papers. Elicit extracts structured data from papers (sample size, methodology, findings). Consensus shows what percentage of studies support a claim. These are qualitatively different from general AI search.

**NotebookLM** (Google) is in a category of its own. You upload your own documents — PDFs, YouTube videos, web links, Google Docs — and it builds an interactive knowledge base around *your sources*. It won't make up facts because it only answers from what you gave it.

**Image generation tools** (Midjourney, DALL-E, Stable Diffusion) are entirely separate neural networks trained on images. You can ask a text AI to describe a picture, but you can't ask it to *generate* one — those are different models with different architectures.

**The principle:** Always use the tool built for your actual job. Using a general chat AI for everything is like using a Swiss Army knife when you have a full kitchen — it works, but it's not optimal.

## The Reasoning Models — A New Category

In 2025-2026, a new category emerged: reasoning models (also called "thinking models"). These models spend extra computation thinking through a problem before responding — dramatically improving accuracy on hard tasks.

**How they differ:** Standard models generate responses in a single pass. Reasoning models have an internal "thinking" phase: they draft, check, revise, and only then produce the visible answer.

**Available reasoning models (2026):**
- **Claude Fable 5** — adaptive thinking always on, can't be disabled; reasoning scales automatically to task difficulty
- **Claude Sonnet 4.6 / Opus 4.8 with Extended Thinking** — activate in Claude.ai (Pro/Max plan)
- **OpenAI o3** — replaced o1 as primary reasoning model at 87% lower cost; o4-mini for budget reasoning tasks
- **Google Gemini 2.5 Pro Deep Think** — explores multiple hypotheses before committing
- **DeepSeek R1** — unique: streams thinking chain inline so you can watch it reason (free at chat.deepseek.com)

**When they're worth using:**
- Complex mathematical or logical problems
- Multi-step analysis where errors compound
- Strategic planning with many constraints
- Contract or legal review requiring careful reasoning

**When standard models are better:**
- Straightforward writing tasks
- Quick summaries and reformatting
- High-volume tasks (reasoning models are 5-20x more expensive per call)

You'll use reasoning mode in Part 13 of this course for complex coding tasks.

## The Tools You'll Actually Use in This Course

You don't need accounts for everything today. Here's what you'll use, and when:

**Starting now (Part 2):**
- **Claude.ai** — Primary tool. Start here.
- **Perplexity.ai** — Part 2. AI research with citations.
- **ChatGPT** — Part 2. Direct comparison.

**During the course:**
- **NotebookLM** — Today's workshop + any time you have documents to learn from
- **Elicit / Consensus** — Part 15 (research track)
- **Gemini** — Part 2 + whenever you use Google Workspace
- **Bing Image Creator** — Part 2. Free image generation, no account needed in Edge
- **Gamma** — Part 16 (presentations)

**Developer track only:**
- **VS Code + GitHub Copilot / Cursor** — Parts 10–11
- **Claude Code** — Part 13. The most powerful tool in the course for technical work
- **Ollama** — Part 18. Local AI models

**Note on accounts:** Sign up for Claude.ai today. You can create the others when you reach their lesson — the course is structured so you always have the tool ready before you need it.

sections.title: Tool Safari — First Contact with 4 Tools
sections.content:
Visit each of these four tools and spend 3-4 minutes with each. The goal is *first contact* — you're not learning them deeply, just building a feel for what each one is and how it's different.

**Stop 1 — Claude.ai** (if you haven't used it yet)
Go to [claude.ai](https://claude.ai). Type:
```
What are three things you can do that a regular Google search can't?
Be specific — give me real examples, not marketing language.
```
Notice: it gives a thoughtful, conversational answer with no links or ads.

**Stop 2 — Perplexity.ai**
Go to [perplexity.ai](https://perplexity.ai). Search for something you genuinely want to know — a current event, a factual question, a topic in your field. Notice:
- Every answer has numbered citations in brackets
- Click one citation — it goes to the original source
- The "Pro Search" option runs more searches for complex questions

This is the fundamental difference from Claude: Perplexity shows its sources in real time.

**Stop 3 — Bing Image Creator** (free, no account needed in Edge browser)
Go to [bing.com/images/create](https://bing.com/images/create). Type:
```
A friendly robot reading a book in a cosy library, warm afternoon light,
digital art, detailed illustration
```
Generate it. This is not text — it's an entirely different kind of AI model producing a visual from your words.

**Stop 4 — NotebookLM**
Go to [notebooklm.google.com](https://notebooklm.google.com) (Google account required). Create a new notebook. Click "Add source" and paste a link to any Wikipedia article you find interesting. Once it processes (30-60 seconds), ask a specific question about a detail in the article. Notice:
- It cites the exact passage it used
- It won't make things up — if the article doesn't cover it, it says so
- Generate an "Audio Overview" to hear a podcast-style summary of your source

**Write one sentence per tool** describing what it does that the others don't. Four sentences total. This is your first draft of a personal AI toolkit.

**Bonus — Elicit.com** (for those interested in academic research):
Go to [elicit.com](https://elicit.com). Type a research question: "Does remote work increase productivity?" or "What interventions reduce employee burnout?" Notice how it searches actual scientific papers and extracts structured findings — not just web articles.

sections.question: You're writing a report that needs to cite current statistics on renewable energy adoption rates. Which tool combination gives you the most reliable, verifiable results?
options: Ask Claude for the statistics — it has comprehensive knowledge
Use Perplexity for the statistics (gives you cited sources you can click and verify) then bring the verified numbers to Claude for analysis and writing
Use Gemini because it's integrated with Google Search
Use ChatGPT Deep Research — it produces the most comprehensive reports
sections.explanation: For statistics that need to be cited and verifiable, Perplexity is the right first step because every statistic comes with a clickable source citation — you can verify the number came from a real, reputable organisation. Claude's knowledge is from training data (potential cutoff issue) and doesn't cite sources by default. Gemini's search integration is good but Perplexity's citation display is cleaner for research purposes. ChatGPT Deep Research is also valid but slower for targeted fact-finding. The key workflow: use a citation-native tool for facts, then bring verified data to Claude for synthesis and writing.

sections.title: Workshop A — AI Tool Landscape Map (Quick Drill)
sections.content:
This 8-minute drill builds your mental map of the AI tool landscape — so you can instantly answer "which AI tool should I use for this?"

**Step 1 — Open a blank document** (Google Docs, Word, or Notion) and draw four columns: "Conversation AI", "Search/Research AI", "Creative AI", "Productivity AI".

**Step 2 — Without looking anything up**, list every AI tool you have heard of under the right column. Aim for 10+ tools total.

**Step 3 — Open Claude.ai** and paste your list. Ask: *"Review my AI tool landscape map. What important tools or categories have I missed? What have I misclassified? Be specific."*

**Step 4 — Update your map** based on Claude's feedback. Add the tools you missed.

**Step 5 — For each column**, identify which single tool you would use first if someone gave you a task in that category. Write the name next to the column header.

**Step 6 — Save your map.** This is your personal AI tools reference — update it as you discover new tools throughout this course.

sections.title: Workshop B — Build an AI Tool Recommendation System
sections.content:
You will build a reusable prompt that helps you (or anyone) choose the right AI tool for a given task. This is a genuinely useful tool — you will reference it every time you start a new AI-assisted task.

**Step 1 — Open Claude.ai** and start a new conversation.

**Step 2 — Describe 3 real tasks** from your work or life that you could imagine using AI for. Be specific: not "writing" but "writing weekly status reports for my manager" or not "research" but "researching competitor pricing".

**Step 3 — Ask Claude:** *"For each of these 3 tasks, recommend the best AI tool available in 2026 and explain: (1) why this tool is best for this specific task, (2) one alternative tool and when to use it instead, (3) one thing to watch out for with this tool. Be specific and practical."*

**Step 4 — Review Claude's recommendations.** Do they match what you expected? What surprised you?

**Step 5 — Mandatory AI review:** Paste Claude's recommendations back with this message: *"Review your own tool recommendations above. Play devil's advocate — find 3 specific cases where your recommendation might be wrong or where a different tool would actually be better."*

**Step 6 — Build your personal tool selection guide:** Based on the full exchange, write a short (1 page) guide: "Which AI tool I use for which type of task." Keep this — it will save you time every week.

**Step 7 — Test your guide:** Pick any task from your work today and use your guide to select a tool. Does the guide's recommendation make sense?

sections.title: Workshop C — Head-to-Head Tool Comparison
sections.content:
The best way to understand what makes each AI tool different is to ask them the same thing and compare. This workshop reveals the real differences — not the marketing.

**Step 1 — Choose a real task** from your work that you need to do anyway this week. Something where the quality of the output matters.

**Step 2 — Craft a specific prompt** for the task. Write it clearly with context.

**Step 3 — Run the exact same prompt** in at least two of these: Claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini. Keep tabs open side-by-side.

**Step 4 — Compare the outputs** across these dimensions:
- Length and detail level
- Tone and style
- Accuracy of specific facts (if applicable)
- Usefulness for your actual task
- What each one got wrong or missed

**Step 5 — Ask Claude** to compare the approaches: *"I ran the same prompt in multiple AI tools. Here are the outputs: [paste them]. What are the meaningful differences in their approaches? Which is most useful for [your task] and why?"*

**Step 6 — Write a one-paragraph verdict:** For this type of task, which tool would you use in the future and why? Add this verdict to your tool guide from Workshop B.

sections.title: Workshop D — Your Personal AI Tools Shortlist
sections.content:
Most people end up using 2-3 AI tools regularly. This workshop helps you decide which ones those should be for you specifically.

**Step 1 — Think about your work and life** over the last month. What were the most time-consuming or tedious tasks? List 5-8 of them.

**Step 2 — For each task**, write: (a) which AI tool you have tried or would try, (b) whether you have actually used AI for this task.

**Step 3 — Open Claude.ai** and paste your task list. Ask: *"I want to build a minimal AI tools setup — ideally 2-3 tools that cover my main use cases. Based on this task list, which 2-3 AI tools would you recommend I start with? Explain why these cover my specific needs. What would I miss by not adding a fourth tool?"*

**Step 4 — Decide your shortlist.** Pick 2-3 tools you will actually use starting today.

**Step 5 — Create accounts** (if you haven't already) for your chosen tools. Bookmark them or add them to your browser toolbar.

**Step 6 — Commit to a 2-week experiment:** For the next 2 weeks, use only your shortlisted tools (no adding new ones). This forces you to learn them well before expanding.

sections.question: A colleague asks which AI tool to use for drafting a business proposal. Which answer is most helpful?
options: Use ChatGPT — it's the most popular
It depends: Claude is strong for long documents and nuanced writing; ChatGPT is good if you need web search integrated
Use whichever you have a subscription to
AI tools are roughly equivalent for writing tasks
sections.explanation: Different AI tools have genuine strengths for different tasks. Claude excels at long, nuanced documents and careful reasoning. ChatGPT has integrated web search and image generation. Recommending the right tool requires knowing the task, not just what's popular or available.

sections.question: Which AI tool category is specifically designed for research with cited sources?
sections.explanation: Perplexity, Consensus, Scite and similar tools are specifically built for research with citations — they retrieve current web sources and link every claim to its source. General conversation AI (Claude, ChatGPT) can discuss topics but doesn't automatically cite sources.

sections.content: **You've completed lesson 1-3.** You now have a map of the 2026 AI tools landscape: the big three general assistants (Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini), specialised research tools (Perplexity, Elicit, Consensus), knowledge base tools (NotebookLM, Claude Projects), reasoning models, and the developer tools you'll use later. Everything in this course uses at least one of these tools.
